questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.x: Au comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning gold. Silver's symbol, Ag, comes from the Latin argentum.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.x: Mercury orbits the Sun in just 88 Earth days, the shortest year of any planet.

questions.q: Which gas do plants absorb from the air for photosynthesis?
questions.x: Plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

questions.q: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?
questions.x: Diamond is a form of pure carbon whose atoms are locked in a rigid crystal lattice. It scores 10 on the Mohs scale.

questions.q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
questions.x: Babies are born with about 300 bones, and many of them fuse together as the child grows.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.x: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Adding a second oxygen gives hydrogen peroxide.

questions.q: What force pulls objects toward the center of the Earth?
questions.x: On Earth's surface, gravity makes falling objects accelerate at about 9.8 meters per second every second.

questions.q: At sea level, at what temperature does water boil in degrees Celsius?
questions.x: Water boils at lower temperatures at high altitude because the air pressure is lower, which is why cooking takes longer on mountains.

questions.q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.x: Mars looks red because its soil is rich in iron oxide, which is essentially rust.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.x: Nitrogen is about 78 percent of the air we breathe, while oxygen is only about 21 percent.

questions.q: What is the process by which plants make their own food using sunlight?
questions.x: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in leaves, inside tiny structures called chloroplasts.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.x: The ampere is named after the French physicist Andre-Marie Ampere, a founder of the study of electromagnetism.

questions.q: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
questions.x: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that also gives blood its red color.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.x: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium compounds. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water.

questions.q: What is Earth's only natural satellite?
questions.x: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters per year.

questions.q: Which scientist is famously linked with a falling apple and the law of universal gravitation?
questions.x: Newton published his law of universal gravitation in 1687 in his book Principia.

questions.q: About how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
questions.x: Light covers about 300,000 kilometers every second, fast enough to circle Earth about 7.5 times in one second.

questions.q: At what temperature in degrees Celsius does water freeze at sea level?
questions.x: Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and why pipes can burst in winter.

questions.q: Which gas do humans need to breathe in to survive?
questions.x: Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, a process called cellular respiration.

questions.q: What is the scientific study of living things called?
questions.x: The word biology comes from the Greek words bios (life) and logos (study).

questions.q: Which planet is best known for its spectacular rings?
questions.x: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, ranging from dust grains to boulders.

questions.q: What kind of animal is a dolphin?
questions.x: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and nurse their young with milk, like all mammals.

questions.q: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
questions.x: A bee must visit about two million flowers to make one pound of honey.

questions.q: Which part of a plant absorbs water from the soil?
questions.x: Tiny root hairs greatly increase the surface area available for taking in water and minerals.

questions.q: What is the common name for sodium chloride?
questions.x: Salt is so valuable in history that the word salary is thought to come from the Latin word for salt.

questions.q: Which vitamin does your skin make when exposed to sunlight?
questions.x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth.

questions.q: How many legs does an insect have?
questions.x: All adult insects have six legs and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

questions.q: How many colors are traditionally listed in a rainbow?
questions.x: Newton chose seven colors, red to violet, partly because he linked them to the seven notes of the musical scale.

questions.q: What is the tiny, dense center of an atom called?
questions.x: The nucleus holds nearly all of an atom's mass, yet it is about 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom.

questions.q: Which pair of organs filters waste from the blood to make urine?
questions.x: Your kidneys filter about 180 liters of blood plasma every day.

questions.q: What sound follows a flash of lightning?
questions.x: Thunder is caused by the air being heated so fast that it expands explosively. Light travels faster than sound, so you see lightning first.

questions.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.x: Mercury's symbol, Hg, comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, meaning liquid silver.

questions.q: Counting outward from the Sun, which planet is third?
questions.x: Earth sits in the so-called habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid water on the surface.

questions.q: What do we call animals that eat only plants?
questions.x: Cows, rabbits and elephants are herbivores. Many have specialized stomachs to break down tough plant material.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
questions.x: Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of Earth's atmosphere and nearly half of the mass of Earth's crust.

questions.q: Which force slows down a book sliding across a table?
questions.x: Friction turns some of the sliding object's motion energy into heat, which is why rubbing your hands together warms them.

questions.q: Which scientist wrote On the Origin of Species?
questions.x: Darwin published the book in 1859 after developing his ideas on natural selection for over twenty years.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to see distant stars and planets more clearly?
questions.x: Galileo's improved telescopes in 1609 and 1610 let him see the Moon's craters and the moons of Jupiter.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation DNA stand for?
questions.x: DNA carries the genetic instructions for building and running living things, coiled into a double helix.

questions.q: In computing, what does CPU stand for?
questions.x: The CPU is often called the brain of the computer because it carries out program instructions.

questions.q: What are the smallest units of digital information, the 0s and 1s, called?
questions.x: The word bit is short for binary digit. Eight bits make up one byte.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when molten lava or magma cools and hardens?
questions.x: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks. The name comes from the Latin word for fire.

questions.q: What is the name for molten rock beneath Earth's surface?
questions.x: Magma is called lava once it erupts onto the surface.

questions.q: What is the name of the thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth?
questions.x: The crust is only 5 to 70 km thick, thinner relative to Earth than the skin of an apple is to the fruit.

questions.q: What is mainly responsible for the ocean tides on Earth?
questions.x: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating two tidal bulges. Most coasts see two high tides a day.

questions.q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.x: The femur, or thigh bone, makes up about a quarter of a person's height.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
questions.x: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron. Iron is the most common element on Earth by mass.

questions.q: Roughly how many days does the Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.x: Because the orbit takes about 365.25 days, we add a leap day to the calendar roughly every four years.

questions.q: Which planet has the hottest surface in the solar system?
questions.x: Venus is hotter than Mercury, at about 465 C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.x: One newton is about the weight of a small apple on Earth's surface.

questions.q: What is a young frog with a tail and gills called?
questions.x: A tadpole gradually grows legs, loses its tail and develops lungs in a process called metamorphosis.

questions.q: What is it called when liquid water turns into water vapor?
questions.x: Evaporation from oceans, lakes and plants drives the water cycle that eventually returns as rain and snow.

questions.q: What is it called when water vapor cools and turns into liquid droplets?
questions.x: Clouds form when water vapor condenses onto tiny dust particles in the air.

questions.q: What does a seismograph record?
questions.x: Modern seismographs can detect earthquakes happening on the opposite side of the planet.

questions.q: What does a barometer measure?
questions.x: Falling air pressure often signals approaching storms, while rising pressure usually means fair weather.

questions.q: Which pair of organs do we use to breathe?
questions.x: Your lungs contain around 300 million tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen enters the blood.

questions.q: About how long does the Earth take to rotate once on its axis?
questions.x: Earth's spin gives us day and night. At the equator, the ground moves at roughly 1,670 km/h.

questions.q: What is a recognizable pattern of stars in the night sky called?
questions.x: Astronomers recognize 88 official constellations, including Orion and Ursa Major.

questions.q: Which part of a cell is known as its powerhouse?
questions.x: Mitochondria convert food into ATP, the usable energy molecule of the cell. They have their own small set of DNA.

questions.q: What green pigment in leaves captures sunlight for photosynthesis?
questions.x: Leaves turn red and orange in autumn when chlorophyll breaks down and other pigments show through.

questions.q: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry?
questions.x: Curie won the Physics prize in 1903 and the Chemistry prize in 1911, and is the only person honored in two different sciences.

questions.q: What is the largest animal on Earth?
questions.x: A blue whale's heart is about the size of a small car, and its tongue can weigh as much as an elephant.

questions.q: Which is the fastest land animal?
questions.x: A cheetah can reach about 100 km/h in short bursts, accelerating faster than most sports cars.

questions.q: Among the eight planets, which one is farthest from the Sun?
questions.x: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.

questions.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.x: Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989 while working at the research lab CERN in Switzerland.

questions.q: Which element is the lightest in the universe?
questions.x: Hydrogen is also the most abundant element in the universe and the main fuel of stars.

questions.q: What word describes animals that are mainly active at night?
questions.x: Owls, bats and many mice are nocturnal, with senses adapted for darkness.

questions.q: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
questions.x: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but you cannot easily squeeze it into a smaller volume.

questions.q: What do paleontologists study?
questions.x: Paleontologists piece together the history of life from fossils, some of them hundreds of millions of years old.

questions.q: What object passes between the Sun and the Earth during a solar eclipse?
questions.x: By coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

questions.q: How many teeth does a typical adult human have, including wisdom teeth?
questions.x: Children have 20 baby teeth, which are replaced by permanent teeth.

questions.q: Which gas is used to fill party balloons so they float?
questions.x: Helium is lighter than air. It was first detected in the Sun in 1868, before it was found on Earth.

questions.q: What does a magnetic compass needle point toward?
questions.x: Earth's liquid iron core generates a magnetic field that the needle aligns with.

questions.q: Which vitamin, found in oranges and lemons, helps prevent scurvy?
questions.x: Sailors on long voyages once suffered terribly from scurvy until citrus fruit was added to their diet.

questions.q: What is the SI base unit of mass?
questions.x: The kilogram is the only SI base unit with a prefix in its name.

questions.q: Which natural disaster is the Richter scale used to measure?
questions.x: Charles Richter developed his scale in 1935. Today scientists mostly use a related moment magnitude scale.

questions.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite launched into orbit in 1957?
questions.x: Sputnik 1 was about the size of a beach ball and beeped radio signals for three weeks.

questions.q: What is the process called by which a caterpillar changes into a butterfly?
questions.x: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body is largely broken down and rebuilt into the adult butterfly.

questions.q: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.x: Spiders are arachnids, not insects. They also have two body parts instead of three.

questions.q: What is the layer of gases surrounding the Earth called?
questions.x: Most of the atmosphere's mass sits within the lowest 16 km, the layer where weather happens.

questions.q: What is the scientific study of weather called?
questions.x: Meteorology has nothing to do with meteors. The name comes from a Greek word for things high in the sky.

questions.q: Which organ controls the body's thoughts, memory and movement?
questions.x: The human brain has roughly 86 billion nerve cells, called neurons.

questions.q: What energy source do solar panels convert into electricity?
questions.x: Solar cells use the photovoltaic effect, in which light knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor, usually silicon.

questions.q: Which group of animals is the only one with feathers?
questions.x: Feathers help birds fly, stay warm and attract mates. Their closest living relatives are the crocodiles.

questions.q: What is the name of the famous space telescope launched in 1990?
questions.x: Hubble orbits about 540 km above Earth, above the blurring effect of the atmosphere.

questions.q: A ramp is an example of which simple machine?
questions.x: An inclined plane lets you lift a heavy load with less force over a longer distance.

questions.q: What is the huge explosion of a dying massive star called?
questions.x: A supernova can briefly outshine an entire galaxy and scatters heavy elements like iron into space.

questions.q: What is the basic building block of all living things?
questions.x: The human body contains roughly 30 trillion cells of about 200 different types.

questions.q: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
questions.x: Diamond is pure carbon whose atoms are packed in a very strong crystal structure.

questions.q: Which part of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
questions.x: The colored iris has tiny muscles that open or close the pupil to control light.

questions.q: What type of scientist studies rocks and the structure of the Earth?
questions.x: Geologists read rock layers to learn how Earth has changed over millions of years.

questions.q: Which planet is famous for its bright rings of ice and rock?
questions.x: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice and stretch far wider than the planet itself.

questions.q: What is the force that slows things down when surfaces rub together?
questions.x: Friction turns movement into heat, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.

questions.q: What state of matter is steam?
questions.x: Steam is water that has been heated until it becomes a gas.

questions.q: What is the process of water turning into vapor called?
questions.x: Heat from the Sun makes water evaporate from oceans, lakes and puddles.

questions.q: What is a sudden shaking of the ground called?
questions.x: Earthquakes happen when blocks of Earth's crust slip along a fault.

questions.q: Which vitamin can our skin make with the help of sunlight?
questions.x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

questions.q: Which tool lets you see things too small for the naked eye?
questions.x: Microscopes let scientists study cells and tiny organisms.

questions.q: Which tool is used to look at distant stars and planets?
questions.x: Galileo used an early telescope to see the moons of Jupiter.

questions.q: What is frozen water called?
questions.x: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: About how fast does sound travel through air at room temperature?
questions.x: Sound travels at about 343 meters per second at 20 C, which is why you hear thunder several seconds after seeing lightning.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
questions.x: Carbon has six protons. Its ability to form four bonds makes it the backbone of all known life.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of the thin atmosphere of Mars?
questions.x: About 95 percent of Mars's atmosphere is carbon dioxide, but the air is so thin that pressure is under 1 percent of Earth's.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
questions.x: K comes from kalium, the Latin form of an Arabic word for plant ashes, the original source of potassium compounds.

questions.q: Who published the Sun-centered model of the solar system in 1543?
questions.x: Copernicus's book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was published in the year he died.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 C?
questions.x: A pH of 7 is neutral. Lower values are acidic and higher values are basic.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell carries out photosynthesis?
questions.x: Chloroplasts are thought to descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancient cell.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of energy?
questions.x: The joule is named after English physicist James Prescott Joule. One joule is roughly the energy needed to lift an apple one meter.

questions.q: What are the blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart called?
questions.x: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the high pressure of each heartbeat.

questions.q: Which planet has a day that is longer than its year?
questions.x: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backward.

questions.q: Who created the first widely accepted periodic table in 1869?
questions.x: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and correctly predicted the properties of gallium and germanium.

questions.q: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for balance and coordination?
questions.x: The cerebellum is only about a tenth of the brain's volume but holds more than half of its neurons.

questions.q: Which hormone, made in the pancreas, lowers blood sugar?
questions.x: People with type 1 diabetes cannot make enough insulin and must replace it, as first done in 1922.

questions.q: What is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust?
questions.x: Aluminum was once more valuable than gold because it was so hard to extract, until an electrolysis method was found in 1886.

questions.q: Which scale ranks minerals by hardness from 1 to 10?
questions.x: Friedrich Mohs created the scale in 1812. A fingernail scratches talc, but only a diamond scratches a diamond.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
questions.x: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.q: Who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610?
questions.x: These moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, are still called the Galilean moons.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
questions.x: Pb comes from plumbum, the Latin word for lead, which is also the root of the word plumber.

questions.q: What type of chemical bond involves atoms sharing pairs of electrons?
questions.x: The two hydrogen atoms in an H2 molecule are held together by a single shared pair of electrons.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
questions.x: One hertz is one cycle per second. It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who first proved the existence of radio waves.

questions.q: What does a Geiger counter detect?
questions.x: A Geiger counter clicks each time a particle of radiation ionizes the gas inside its tube.

questions.q: Which monk is known as the father of modern genetics for his experiments on pea plants?
questions.x: Mendel worked in the 1860s, but his findings on inheritance were largely ignored until around 1900.

questions.q: A deficiency of which nutrient can cause night blindness?
questions.x: Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the pigment in the eye that works in dim light. Carrots and sweet potatoes are good sources.

questions.q: What is the main component of natural gas?
questions.x: Methane has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms (CH4). Natural gas has no smell, so a harmless odor is added for safety.

questions.q: What is the common name for sodium bicarbonate?
questions.x: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with acid, which makes cakes and breads rise.

questions.q: What does a light-year measure?
questions.x: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered the electron in 1897?
questions.x: Thomson's cathode ray experiments showed that atoms contain smaller, negatively charged particles.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.x: We inherit 23 chromosomes from each parent, making 23 pairs in total.

questions.q: Which layer at the back of the eye detects light and sends signals to the brain?
questions.x: The retina holds about 120 million rod cells for dim light and about 6 million cone cells for color.

questions.q: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
questions.x: At absolute zero, 0 kelvin, particles have the lowest possible energy. Nothing in nature has been cooled to exactly that point.

questions.q: Which planet spins on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees?
questions.x: Uranus's odd tilt means each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

questions.q: What type of wave is sound in air?
questions.x: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate back and forth along the direction the wave travels. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Sn?
questions.x: Sn comes from stannum, the Latin word for tin. Tin mixed with copper makes bronze.

questions.q: Which organ produces bile to help digest fats?
questions.x: The liver makes bile, and the gallbladder stores and concentrates it. The liver also has a remarkable ability to regrow.

questions.q: On which planet is Olympus Mons, the tallest known volcano in the solar system?
questions.x: Olympus Mons is about 22 km tall, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level.

questions.q: What is the scientific study of earthquakes called?
questions.x: Seismologists also use earthquake waves to map Earth's interior, which is how the liquid outer core was discovered.

questions.q: Which scale is used to classify hurricanes by wind speed?
questions.x: The Saffir-Simpson scale has five categories, and Category 5 means sustained winds of at least 157 mph.

questions.q: Which element makes up pure diamonds and graphite?
questions.x: Diamond and graphite differ only in how their carbon atoms are arranged. Graphite is soft enough to write with.

questions.q: What instrument measures wind speed?
questions.x: Most anemometers use spinning cups. The first one was described by Leon Battista Alberti around 1450.

questions.q: Which English physician described the circulation of blood in 1628?
questions.x: Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood in a loop around the body, overturning ideas that dated back to ancient Greece.

questions.q: Which large spiral galaxy is the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way?
questions.x: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and is moving toward us. It is expected to merge with the Milky Way in billions of years.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission made the first crewed Moon landing?
questions.x: Apollo 11 landed in July 1969, and the astronauts spent about 21 hours on the surface.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.x: The ohm is named after Georg Ohm, who showed that current is proportional to voltage in a conductor.

questions.q: What are the two main metals in Earth's core?
questions.x: The solid inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, around 5,000 to 6,000 C.

questions.q: Which noble gas has the chemical symbol Ar?
questions.x: Argon makes up almost 1 percent of Earth's air. Its name comes from the Greek word for lazy, because it barely reacts.

questions.q: In computing, what does RAM stand for?
questions.x: RAM is a computer's short-term working memory, and its contents are lost when the power is switched off.

questions.q: Who is often called the first computer programmer for her notes on the Analytical Engine?
questions.x: In 1843 Lovelace published an algorithm meant for Charles Babbage's machine, which was never completed in his lifetime.

questions.q: How many bits are in one byte?
questions.x: A single byte can represent 256 different values, enough for one letter in the ASCII character set.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula of ozone?
questions.x: Ozone is made of three oxygen atoms. Near the ground it is a pollutant, but high up it shields us from ultraviolet light.

questions.q: In which cell structures are proteins assembled?
questions.x: Ribosomes read messenger RNA and link amino acids together in the correct order. A human cell can contain millions of them.

questions.q: What is the largest artery in the human body?
questions.x: The aorta is about as wide as a garden hose and carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body.

questions.q: Which component of blood is most important for clotting?
questions.x: Platelets are tiny cell fragments that stick together at a wound to form a plug.

questions.q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
questions.x: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, so light from it takes over four years to reach us.

questions.q: Marble is an example of which type of rock?
questions.x: Marble forms when limestone is changed by intense heat and pressure deep in the Earth.

questions.q: Which physicist is known for the uncertainty principle of quantum mechanics?
questions.x: Heisenberg's 1927 principle says you cannot know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle at the same time.

questions.q: What is the bending of light as it passes from air into water called?
questions.x: Refraction is why a straw in a glass of water appears bent and why lenses can focus light.

questions.q: Which isotope is used to date ancient organic remains up to about 50,000 years old?
questions.x: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, so after roughly 50,000 years too little remains to measure accurately.

questions.q: The thyroid and adrenal glands belong to which body system?
questions.x: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate growth, metabolism and mood.

questions.q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid?
questions.x: Dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, sublimes at room pressure, which is why it leaves no puddle.

questions.q: Which nonmetal element is liquid at room temperature?
questions.x: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature and normal pressure. Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid with a sharp smell.

questions.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.x: Enamel is about 96 percent mineral. It cannot regrow because it contains no living cells.

questions.q: Which French physicist discovered radioactivity in 1896?
questions.x: Becquerel noticed that uranium salts fogged photographic plates even without light. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize with the Curies.

questions.q: Which planet is the least dense, with an average density lower than water?
questions.x: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm3, so in theory it would float in a bathtub big enough to hold it.

questions.q: What is the SI base unit of temperature?
questions.x: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so it has no negative values.

questions.q: Which gas gives rotten eggs their smell?
questions.x: Humans can smell hydrogen sulfide at extremely low concentrations, but at high levels it dulls the sense of smell and is toxic.

questions.q: Which type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
questions.x: The Milky Way has a bar of stars across its center, and the Sun lies in one of its spiral arms.

questions.q: What was the name of the supercontinent that existed about 300 million years ago?
questions.x: Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago, and the pieces slowly drifted into today's continents.

questions.q: Who proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912?
questions.x: Wegener was dismissed for decades because he could not explain the mechanism, but plate tectonics later proved him right.

questions.q: Which layer of the Earth is made of liquid metal?
questions.x: Swirling motion in the liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.q: Which instrument measures the amount of moisture in the air?
questions.x: The hair hygrometer works because human hair gets slightly longer in humid air.

questions.q: What primarily causes the seasons on Earth?
questions.x: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered the neutron in 1932?
questions.x: Chadwick won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. Neutrons became the key to nuclear fission.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
questions.x: One pascal is a very small pressure, about the weight of a sheet of paper lying flat on a table.

questions.q: What is the process of cell division that produces two identical body cells?
questions.x: Mitosis is how you grow and heal wounds, while meiosis is the special division that makes sex cells.

questions.q: Which blood type is considered the universal red cell donor?
questions.x: O negative red cells lack the A, B and Rh markers, so they can usually be given to anyone in an emergency.

questions.q: What is the visible surface layer of the Sun called?
questions.x: The photosphere is about 5,500 C. The corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, is paradoxically millions of degrees hotter.

questions.q: What type of star is our Sun?
questions.x: Our Sun is a main-sequence star that is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its lifetime.

questions.q: Which gas is the second most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.x: Early Earth had almost no free oxygen. It built up after bacteria began photosynthesizing more than 2 billion years ago.

questions.q: What name is given to the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion?
questions.x: Inertia is why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly. Newton's first law describes it.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation LED stand for?
questions.x: LEDs turn electricity into light far more efficiently than old incandescent bulbs, which waste most of their energy as heat.

questions.q: What does HTTP stand for in web addresses?
questions.x: HTTP defines how browsers request pages from servers. The secure version, HTTPS, encrypts the connection.

questions.q: Which astronomer discovered the three laws of planetary motion?
questions.x: Kepler's first law showed that planets move in ellipses, not perfect circles. He built his laws from Brahe's precise observations.

questions.q: Which molecule carries genetic instructions from DNA to the ribosomes?
questions.x: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is the copy of a gene that ribosomes read to build a protein.

questions.q: Which mineral is the main component of bones and teeth?
questions.x: About 99 percent of the calcium in your body is stored in your bones and teeth.

questions.q: What is the process by which plants release water vapor from their leaves?
questions.x: A large tree can release hundreds of liters of water into the air on a hot day through tiny leaf pores called stomata.

questions.q: In which organ does most nutrient absorption take place?
questions.x: The small intestine is about 6 meters long, and its folded lining gives it a surface area of roughly a tennis court.

questions.q: Around which planet does the moon Europa orbit?
questions.x: Europa has an ice shell covering a salty ocean that may hold twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.x: One watt equals one joule per second. The unit honors James Watt, who improved the steam engine.

questions.q: Which two scientists proposed the double helix structure of DNA in 1953?
questions.x: Their model drew on X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins's group.

questions.q: What is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter?
questions.x: Ceres is about 940 km across and holds roughly a third of the belt's total mass.

questions.q: Which type of cloud is thin, wispy and found high in the sky?
questions.x: Cirrus clouds are made of ice crystals and often appear before a change in the weather.

questions.q: What is the Sun's thin outer atmosphere, visible during a total solar eclipse, called?
questions.x: The corona is over a million degrees, far hotter than the Sun's surface, and scientists are still studying why.

questions.q: A magnifying glass uses what kind of lens?
questions.x: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and bends light rays together to a focus.

questions.q: Which protein in red blood cells carries oxygen?
questions.x: Each hemoglobin molecule can bind four oxygen molecules, and it contains iron.

questions.q: What form of energy does a moving object have?
questions.x: Kinetic energy equals one half of mass times speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples it.

questions.q: What is the region around Earth dominated by its magnetic field called?
questions.x: The magnetosphere deflects most of the solar wind and is why we see auroras near the poles.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
questions.x: Table salt is sodium chloride, made of sodium and chlorine.

questions.q: Which particle in an atom has a negative electric charge?
questions.x: Electrons carry a negative charge, protons a positive one, and neutrons none.

questions.q: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion?
questions.x: Newton published his laws of motion in 1687 in the Principia.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water at room temperature?
questions.x: A pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of gold?
questions.x: Gold's atomic number is 79, meaning each atom has 79 protons. Silver is 47, lead is 82 and copper is 29.

questions.q: Which metal has the highest melting point of all metals, about 3,400 C?
questions.x: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 C, which is why it was used for filaments in incandescent light bulbs.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the solar system?
questions.x: Io is squeezed and stretched by Jupiter's gravity, which heats its interior and drives hundreds of active volcanoes.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn shoots plumes of water ice from cracks near its south pole?
questions.x: The Cassini spacecraft flew through Enceladus's geysers, finding salty water and organic molecules.

questions.q: Who discovered the planet Uranus in 1781?
questions.x: Herschel first thought it was a comet. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.x: The tesla honors Nikola Tesla. A typical MRI scanner uses a magnetic field of 1.5 to 3 tesla.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of radioactivity, equal to one decay per second?
questions.x: The becquerel is named after Henri Becquerel. One becquerel is very small, so large sources are measured in megabecquerels.

questions.q: Which SI unit measures the absorbed dose of ionizing radiation?
questions.x: One gray is one joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of matter. It is named after physicist Louis Harold Gray.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical capacitance?
questions.x: The farad is named after Michael Faraday. Most real capacitors are measured in microfarads or smaller.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of inductance?
questions.x: The henry is named after the American scientist Joseph Henry, who discovered self-induction in the 1830s.

questions.q: Which SI base unit measures luminous intensity?
questions.x: The candela was originally defined using the light of a standard candle, hence the name.

questions.q: Which SI base unit measures the amount of a substance?
questions.x: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 x 10^23 particles, a number known as Avogadro's constant.

questions.q: What is the freezing point of water on the Kelvin scale?
questions.x: A change of one kelvin is exactly the same size as a change of one degree Celsius. The two scales differ only in their zero point.

questions.q: Which part of the brain acts as the main relay station for sensory signals heading to the cortex?
questions.x: Nearly all sensory information except smell passes through the thalamus on its way to the cerebral cortex.

questions.q: Which cell organelle contains digestive enzymes that break down waste?
questions.x: Lysosomes contain about 50 types of enzymes and work best in acidic conditions.

questions.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix before replication?
questions.x: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, working like a zipper being opened.

questions.q: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA instead of thymine?
questions.x: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, and pairs it with adenine.

questions.q: What is the medical name for the collarbone?
questions.x: The clavicle is the most commonly broken bone in children. Its name comes from the Latin for little key.

questions.q: What is the longest nerve in the human body?
questions.x: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down each leg and is as thick as a finger.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three tiny bones of the middle ear?
questions.x: The incus, malleus and stapes are also known as the anvil, hammer and stirrup, and they are the smallest bones in the body.

questions.q: Vitamin B12 contains which metal ion at its center?
questions.x: B12 is also called cobalamin because of the cobalt atom at its core. Only microorganisms can make it.

questions.q: What is the most abundant protein in mammals?
questions.x: Collagen makes up about a quarter of the protein in the human body and gives skin, tendons and bones their strength.

questions.q: Which gas is the third most abundant in Earth's dry atmosphere, at about 0.9 percent?
questions.x: Argon is produced mainly by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in Earth's crust.

questions.q: After oxygen, which element is the second most abundant in Earth's crust by mass?
questions.x: Silicon makes up about 28 percent of the crust, mostly locked in silicate minerals and quartz.

questions.q: What is the Mohs hardness of quartz?
questions.x: Quartz is harder than steel and glass. Only topaz, corundum and diamond score higher on the scale.

questions.q: Which scale has largely replaced the Richter scale for measuring large earthquakes?
questions.x: The moment magnitude scale measures the total energy released and does not saturate for the biggest quakes.

questions.q: Which type of seismic wave arrives first at a recording station?
questions.x: P stands for primary. These compression waves travel through solids and liquids, while slower S-waves cannot pass through liquid.

questions.q: In which hemisphere does the Coriolis effect deflect moving air to the right?
questions.x: This deflection makes large storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.

questions.q: Which cloud type is responsible for thunderstorms?
questions.x: Cumulonimbus clouds can tower more than 12 km high and are the only cloud type that produces thunder and lightning.

questions.q: What is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere called?
questions.x: Commercial jets often cruise near the tropopause, where the air is smooth and thin.

questions.q: In which atmospheric layer do most auroras occur?
questions.x: Auroras glow roughly 100 to 300 km up, where charged particles from the Sun collide with oxygen and nitrogen.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first to enter interstellar space, in 2012?
questions.x: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is the most distant human-made object from Earth.

questions.q: Which star appears brightest in Earth's night sky, not counting the Sun?
questions.x: Sirius, in the constellation Canis Major, is about 8.6 light-years away and is actually a pair of stars.

questions.q: What will the Sun become after its red giant phase ends?
questions.x: The Sun is too small to explode as a supernova. It will shed its outer layers and leave a dense core about the size of Earth.

questions.q: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape called?
questions.x: The event horizon is not a physical surface. It is the point where the escape velocity equals the speed of light.

questions.q: Which astronomer's observations in the 1920s showed that the universe is expanding?
questions.x: Hubble found that distant galaxies are receding faster the farther away they are, and published the relation in 1929.

questions.q: About how old is the universe?
questions.x: The estimate comes from measurements of the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate of the universe.

questions.q: About how old is the Earth?
questions.x: The age is derived from radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks, which give about 4.54 billion years.

questions.q: What did Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson accidentally discover in 1964?
questions.x: They first blamed the faint microwave hiss on pigeon droppings in their antenna. It turned out to be leftover radiation from the early universe.

questions.q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic force?
questions.x: Photons also make up visible light, and they have no mass or electric charge.

questions.q: How many quarks make up a proton?
questions.x: A proton contains two up quarks and one down quark held together by gluons.

questions.q: Which European research organization operates the Large Hadron Collider?
questions.x: The LHC's 27-kilometer ring lies beneath the border of France and Switzerland. The Higgs boson was found there in 2012.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
questions.x: Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field creates an electric current, the principle behind generators and transformers.

questions.q: Who discovered in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic field?
questions.x: Orsted noticed a compass needle twitch near a wire carrying current during a lecture demonstration.

questions.q: Which physicist proposed in 1913 that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels?
questions.x: Bohr's model explained why hydrogen emits light only at specific colors.

questions.q: Whose gold foil experiment showed that atoms have a small, dense nucleus?
questions.x: A few alpha particles bounced almost straight back, which Rutherford compared to a shell bouncing off tissue paper.

questions.q: Which element did Marie Curie name in honor of her homeland?
questions.x: Curie announced polonium in 1898, naming it after Poland, which was then partitioned between three empires.

questions.q: Which element with atomic number 99 is named after a famous physicist?
questions.x: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the 1952 hydrogen bomb test, and was kept secret for several years.

questions.q: Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.x: Fluorine pulls electrons so strongly that it reacts with almost every other element, including some noble gases.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH range of human stomach acid?
questions.x: Stomach acid is mostly hydrochloric acid, strong enough to dissolve some metals. A thick layer of mucus protects the stomach lining.

questions.q: Which acid is used in lead-acid car batteries?
questions.x: A lead-acid battery has plates of lead immersed in dilute sulfuric acid. The design dates from 1859.

questions.q: Which noble gas has the lowest boiling point of all elements?
questions.x: Helium boils at about -269 C, only 4 degrees above absolute zero, and never freezes at normal pressure.

questions.q: Which is the lightest metal?
questions.x: Lithium is so light that it floats on water, and it is used in rechargeable batteries.

questions.q: The alloy bronze is made mainly of copper and which other metal?
questions.x: The Bronze Age began around 3300 BC when people learned that adding tin made copper harder.

questions.q: The alloy brass is made mainly of copper and which other metal?
questions.x: Brass is bright and easy to shape, and its sound qualities make it the traditional material for horns.

questions.q: Which naturalist independently came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection, prompting Darwin to publish?
questions.x: Wallace sent Darwin his essay from the Malay Archipelago in 1858, and their ideas were presented together to the Linnean Society.

questions.q: Which German chemist is said to have discovered the ring structure of benzene after a daydream?
questions.x: Kekule said he envisioned a snake biting its own tail in 1865, which gave him the idea of a closed ring of carbon atoms.

questions.q: Which French chemist is known as the father of modern chemistry and the law of conservation of mass?
questions.x: Lavoisier named oxygen and hydrogen. He was guillotined during the French Revolution in 1794.

questions.q: Which Danish astronomer used Jupiter's moons to estimate the speed of light in 1676?
questions.x: Romer noticed that eclipses of Io ran late when Jupiter was farther from Earth, proving that light takes time to travel.

questions.q: Which two Swiss astronomers discovered the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star, in 1995?
questions.x: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b and shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

questions.q: Which Greek scholar estimated the Earth's circumference around 240 BC using shadows?
questions.x: He compared the Sun's angle at two Egyptian cities and got a result within a few percent of the real value.

questions.q: Whose experiments with swan-neck flasks helped disprove spontaneous generation?
questions.x: In the 1860s, Pasteur showed that broth stayed clear as long as airborne germs could not reach it.

questions.q: Which pair of Canadian researchers is credited with discovering insulin in 1921?
questions.x: Frederick Banting and Charles Best worked in Toronto. Banting shared the 1923 Nobel Prize with J.J.R. Macleod.

questions.q: Which mathematician described an abstract model of computation in 1936, now called a Turing machine?
questions.x: Turing's model defined what it means for a problem to be computable. He also helped break the German Enigma code in World War II.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation ASCII stand for?
a: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Advanced System Code for Internet Integration
Automatic Symbol Coding for Input Interfaces
Applied Standard Computing and Information Interface
questions.x: ASCII assigns numbers to letters and symbols. The original version used 7 bits, giving 128 characters.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
questions.x: A 32-bit address allows about 4.3 billion unique addresses, which is why the longer 128-bit IPv6 was created.

questions.q: The hexadecimal number system is base what?
questions.x: Hexadecimal uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. Programmers use it because one hex digit equals exactly four bits.

questions.q: How many meters are in one international nautical mile?
questions.x: A nautical mile equals one minute of latitude, and a speed of one nautical mile per hour is one knot.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
questions.x: One ampere of current is one coulomb of charge flowing past a point each second.

questions.q: What is the approximate escape velocity from Earth's surface?
questions.x: An object must travel at about 11.2 km/s to break free of Earth's gravity without further propulsion. That is more than 40,000 km/h.

questions.q: What scattering effect makes the daytime sky blue?
questions.x: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more strongly than long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from all directions.

questions.q: Which gas law states that, at constant temperature, pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional?
questions.x: Robert Boyle published his law in 1662. It explains why a scuba diver's lungs expand while ascending.

questions.q: Which cell organelle makes lipids and has no ribosomes attached?
questions.x: The smooth ER also helps detoxify chemicals, which is why liver cells have a lot of it.

questions.q: To which biological kingdom do mushrooms belong?
questions.x: Fungi are genetically closer to animals than to plants. They digest food outside their bodies and absorb it.

questions.q: What term describes organisms that make their own food from simple substances?
questions.x: Plants, algae and some bacteria are autotrophs. Most make food using sunlight, while others use chemical energy.

questions.q: Jellyfish belong to which animal phylum?
questions.x: Cnidarians, including jellyfish, corals and sea anemones, have stinging cells called cnidocytes.

questions.q: Which bird is the fastest animal in a dive, exceeding 300 km/h?
questions.x: Peregrine falcons have been clocked at over 320 km/h during their hunting dives, called stoops.

questions.q: What is the largest cell in the human body?
questions.x: The ovum is about 0.1 mm across and just visible to the naked eye. Sperm cells are among the smallest.

questions.q: Which glands sit on top of the kidneys and release adrenaline?
questions.x: The adrenal glands also make cortisol, the hormone linked with the body's response to stress.

questions.q: Which muscle is the largest in the human body?
questions.x: The gluteus maximus is the main muscle for standing up from a seated position and climbing stairs.

questions.q: What are the two upper chambers of the heart called?
questions.x: The atria receive blood returning to the heart, and the stronger ventricles pump it out.

questions.q: Which flap of tissue covers the windpipe when you swallow?
questions.x: The epiglottis closes over the airway during swallowing, so food and drink slide down the esophagus instead.

questions.q: Which white blood cells produce antibodies?
questions.x: B cells mature in bone marrow, which is where the B comes from in the older name bursa-derived. Each B cell makes just one type of antibody.

questions.q: Which hormone, also called epinephrine, prepares the body for fight or flight?
questions.x: Adrenaline speeds the heart, widens the airways and sends extra blood to the muscles within seconds.

questions.q: Which English scientist first used the word cell for living things after viewing cork under a microscope in 1665?
questions.x: Hooke thought the tiny compartments in cork resembled the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in.

questions.q: Which three American physicists invented the transistor at Bell Labs in 1947?
questions.x: The transistor replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made modern electronics possible. The trio shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: The Haber process is used to industrially produce which compound?
questions.x: The Haber process combines nitrogen from the air with hydrogen, making the fertilizer that helps feed billions of people.

questions.q: What is the approximate temperature at the Sun's core?
questions.x: At the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing the energy that powers the Sun.

questions.q: What is the larger of Mars's two moons?
questions.x: Phobos orbits so close to Mars that it circles the planet three times a day and is slowly spiraling inward.

questions.q: Which large moon of Neptune orbits in the opposite direction to the planet's rotation?
questions.x: Triton's backward orbit suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. It has nitrogen geysers and is one of the coldest known places in the solar system.

questions.q: What was the name of the lander that touched down on comet 67P in 2014?
questions.x: Philae was carried by the European probe Rosetta and made the first soft landing on a comet.

questions.q: How many hexagonal mirror segments make up the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror?
questions.x: The segments are coated in a thin layer of gold, which reflects infrared light well. The mirror unfolded after launch.

questions.q: What is the average distance from Earth to the Moon?
questions.x: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth.

questions.q: Roughly how long is one astronomical unit, the average distance from Earth to the Sun?
questions.x: One astronomical unit is about 150 million km, or 93 million miles. Neptune orbits at about 30 AU.

questions.q: What is Avogadro's number, approximately?
questions.x: It is the number of particles in one mole of a substance. 12 grams of carbon-12 contain this many atoms.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle in an atom has the least mass?
questions.x: A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron.

questions.q: Which element makes up the largest share of the human body's mass?
questions.x: Oxygen is about 65 percent of body mass, mostly because the body is so rich in water. Carbon is next at about 18 percent.

questions.q: What is the longest phase of the cell cycle called?
questions.x: Cells spend most of their lives in interphase, growing and copying their DNA, and only a small fraction of time dividing.

questions.q: Which British chemist isolated sodium and potassium by electrolysis in 1807?
questions.x: Davy reportedly danced around his lab with joy when he saw tiny globules of potassium form and burst into flame.

questions.q: Which Greek letter is the standard symbol for wavelength in physics?
questions.x: Wavelength, written as lambda, multiplied by frequency gives the speed of a wave.
